subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; aalii is indigenous across Hawaiian leeward dry forest and tolerates wind, salt, and long dry spells once established.

directions: Aalii is a tough, fine-textured evergreen shrub with narrow leaves and papery, winged seed capsules that turn rose-pink to coppery-red on female plants, a feature that has made the cultivar 'Purpurea' a popular dryland landscape shrub. It thrives in poor, rocky, fast-draining soil and full sun, needing little supplemental water once roots are established, and responds well to pruning as an informal hedge or windbreak. Seed benefits from a hot-water soak to break the hard seed coat before sowing, while cuttings let growers select female plants for their showier seed capsules. Avoid heavy, wet soils and overly rich fertilizer, which encourage lanky, weak growth in this otherwise resilient Pacific native.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources
Hui Kū Maoli Ola Native Hawaiian Plant Specialists
USDA Forest Service Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained volcanic or rocky soil in full sun; naio tolerates thin, dry dry-forest substrates and wind-exposed leeward sites once its root system is established.

directions: Naio earned its 'false sandalwood' name from early traders who substituted its fragrant wood for true sandalwood, and it ranges from a dense small tree to a gnarled dry-forest shrub depending on site conditions. Clusters of small white to pale pink, faintly sweet-smelling tubular flowers appear through most of the year, followed by small fleshy fruit favored by native birds. Because seed can take many months to sprout and germinates unevenly, growers who want uniform landscape stock generally propagate naio from cuttings or air layers instead. Give it lean, sharply drained soil and full sun, and avoid overwatering, which this dry-forest native tolerates poorly.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest shrub berry

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; ulei is a tough colonizer of dry lava fields and disturbed leeward slopes and establishes easily on poor ground.

directions: Ulei is a rose-family shrub that grows either as a low, trailing groundcover over rock and lava or as an upright multi-stemmed shrub, making it adaptable to many garden roles from bank stabilization to informal hedging. Small white, five-petaled flowers cluster at branch tips through much of the year and ripen into tiny white, apple-like fruit that birds strip quickly and that Hawaiians historically ate in modest amounts. It is remarkably unfussy about soil fertility and competes well on disturbed or rocky ground, needing only good drainage and sun to thrive. Light pruning after fruiting keeps spreading forms tidy without reducing next season's bloom.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest flowering tree

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nicked/soaked seed in spring into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; wiliwili is adapted to leeward dry-forest sites below about 2,000 feet elevation and sheds its leaves during the dry season before flowering.

directions: Wiliwili is a stout, gnarled dry-forest tree endemic to Hawaii that drops its leaves in the dry season and then bursts into bloom on bare branches, producing curved, hook-shaped flowers in shades ranging from salmon and orange to pale green or cream depending on the individual tree. Seed has a hard coat and germinates faster after a brief soak or light scarification, while cuttings offer a quicker, truer way to propagate a particular flower color. It needs full sun, excellent drainage, and tolerates long dry periods well once established, but resents soggy or heavy soil. Historically its lightweight wood was carved into surfboards and canoe outriggers, and the tree remains a dramatic specimen for dry, frost-free gardens.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest flowering tree

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring into lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; mamane grows naturally in dry montane woodlands and tolerates occasional cold and even light frost far better than most Hawaiian natives.

directions: Mamane is a Hawaiian-endemic legume tree with soft, pinnate silver-green foliage and curved, bright yellow pea flowers borne mainly in winter and spring, prized historically as critical forage for native birds like the palila. It is one of the more cold-tolerant Hawaiian dry forest natives, naturally ranging into montane woodland where frost occurs, which makes it unusually forgiving for a tropical-island endemic. Untreated seed germinates poorly, so growers typically nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat before sowing to improve and speed emergence. Give it rocky, sharply drained, low-fertility soil and full sun, and expect a slow-growing but long-lived small tree that resents wet feet.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources
USDA Forest Service Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry

subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest flowering shrub

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or transplants in spring into sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun; ilima grows naturally from dry coastal flats into dry forest and flowers nearly continuously in warm, sunny conditions.

directions: Ilima, the official flower of Oahu, bears a steady flush of delicate golden-orange, hibiscus-like blooms that each last only a single day but are produced in such abundance that the plant appears to flower year-round in warm, sunny spots. It ranges from a low, silvery-leaved coastal groundcover to a more upright shrub form, and named selections are usually propagated by cuttings to keep flower color and habit consistent. Because each tiny, paper-thin blossom must be strung individually, ilima lei have traditionally been reserved for royalty and remain prized as one of the most labor-intensive Hawaiian lei flowers. Give it lean, sandy, well-drained soil and full sun, and avoid rich fertilizer or heavy shade, both of which reduce flowering.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest flowering shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; mao is endemic to dry coastal and lowland dry-forest Hawaiian habitats and tolerates salt spray and extended drought well.

directions: Mao is a low, wide-spreading shrub covered in velvety, silver-gray foliage that sets it apart from cultivated cotton, with bright yellow flowers opening from late summer into winter followed by small cotton bolls bearing brownish lint. It is valued by plant breeders as a source of drought and salt tolerance genes for commercial cotton improvement, but it also makes an attractive, low-maintenance silver-foliage accent for dry, sunny gardens outside Hawaii. Seed germinates quickly without special treatment and seedlings establish fast in lean, sharply drained soil. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil and crowding, both of which encourage fungal problems in this otherwise tough coastal dry-forest native.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest flowering shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring into lean, rocky, fast-draining soil in full sun; maiapilo grows naturally on dry coastal cliffs and lowland dry-forest rock outcrops and resents any standing moisture.

directions: Maiapilo is a sprawling, trailing Hawaiian-endemic shrub whose large, white, crepe-paper flowers open only after dusk and release a sweet fragrance along with a dramatic spray of long purple-tinged stamens, then wilt by mid-morning, making it a striking choice for a dry-garden night-bloom border. It is now vulnerable in the wild, threatened by grazing animals and invasive competitors, but remains in cultivation through Hawaiian native-plant nurseries and botanical gardens. Seed germination is slow and uneven, so patience and consistently warm, dry-draining conditions help improve results. Grow it over rock or on a sunny slope where its sprawling stems can drape naturally, and avoid any soil that stays wet after rain.
sources: Hui Kū Maoli Ola Native Hawaiian Plant Specialists
